subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Study of a set drama text

questions.q: In this 'open text' drama paper, what are candidates permitted to do?
options: Take a clean, unannotated copy of the set text into the examination
Take fully annotated notes and essay plans into the examination
Answer entirely from memory with no text available
Access an online copy of the play during the examination
questions.explain: 'Open text' means candidates may use a clean, unmarked copy of the set drama text in the exam, but not annotations or notes.

questions.q: What is printed on the examination paper for a passage-based (extract) question?
options: A specific extract from the set drama text
A summary of the whole play
A list of critical quotations about the play
An unseen extract from a different play
questions.explain: The passage-based question prints a chosen extract from the studied play for candidates to analyse closely.

questions.q: How does an essay (whole-text) question differ from a passage-based question?
options: It provides no printed extract and asks candidates to draw on the whole play
It prints a longer extract than the passage-based question
It requires candidates to write about an unseen text
It is marked without reference to the assessment objectives
questions.explain: The essay (discursive) question gives no extract and expects candidates to range across the whole drama text.

questions.q: What is a soliloquy in a drama text?
options: A speech by a character alone on stage, revealing their thoughts to the audience
A rapid exchange of dialogue between two characters
A remark aimed at the audience while others are present
An instruction in the script describing stage movement
questions.explain: A soliloquy is delivered by a character alone on stage, giving the audience access to their private thoughts.

options: When the audience knows something that a character on stage does not
When a character speaks directly to the audience
When the ending contradicts the play's opening
When two characters misunderstand each other's words
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises when the audience possesses knowledge that a character lacks, creating tension or poignancy.

options: A brief remark spoken so that some characters on stage do not hear it
A lengthy speech by a character standing alone
A description of the stage setting
The division of a play into acts
questions.explain: An aside is a short remark, often to the audience, that other characters on stage are conventionally assumed not to hear.

options: Instructions in the script describing setting, action, movement or delivery
The spoken lines exchanged between characters
A character's private reflections spoken aloud
The list of characters at the start of the play
questions.explain: Stage directions are the playwright's instructions about setting, movement, gesture and delivery, distinct from spoken dialogue.

questions.q: Why is close reference to the wording essential in a passage-based response?
options: Because the question rewards analysis of how the playwright's language and methods create effects in the extract
Because candidates must copy out the whole extract to gain marks
Because the extract must be summarised in order to show knowledge
Because context of the writer's life is the main focus
questions.explain: Passage-based answers require detailed engagement with the specific language and dramatic methods of the printed extract.

questions.q: What does a strong essay (whole-text) response chiefly demonstrate?
options: A sustained argument supported by references drawn from across the whole play
A detailed line-by-line analysis of a single printed extract
Memorised biographical facts about the playwright
A retelling of the plot in chronological order
questions.explain: The essay question rewards a focused, developed argument evidenced by well-selected references from across the drama.

questions.q: What is the main dramatic purpose of a soliloquy?
options: To let the audience share a character's inner thoughts and motives
To speed up the pace of the action on stage
To introduce a new character to the audience
To signal the end of an act
questions.explain: A soliloquy gives the audience privileged insight into a character's inner conflict, feelings and intentions.

questions.q: When responding to a printed extract, what should candidates focus on most?
options: How the playwright uses language, structure and dramatic methods to shape meaning and effect
How the extract could be improved by rewriting it
How the plot continues after the extract ends
How many characters appear in the play as a whole
questions.explain: Extract responses should explore the writer's craft, showing how methods create particular effects for the audience.

questions.q: What is meant by an 'informed personal response' to a drama text?
options: A considered individual viewpoint grounded in evidence from the text
An emotional reaction with no reference to the play
A summary of what critics have argued about the play
A word-for-word recall of key speeches
questions.explain: An informed personal response combines a candidate's own judgement with support drawn from the text itself.

questions.q: Why does an essay question demand secure knowledge of the whole play?
options: Because candidates must select relevant references from different points in the drama to build their argument
Because only the final scene is examined in essays
Because the extract is hidden until the exam begins
Because essays are marked purely on length
questions.explain: Without a printed extract, essay answers rely on the candidate's overview and precise recall of the whole text.

questions.q: What effect does dramatic irony most commonly create for an audience?
options: Tension or suspense as the audience anticipates what a character cannot foresee
Confusion about the identity of the characters
A slowing of the plot to allow scene changes
A comic misunderstanding that resolves immediately
questions.explain: Because the audience knows more than the character, dramatic irony heightens tension, suspense or pathos.

questions.q: A candidate answering a passage-based question copies large sections of the extract and retells the plot. What should they do instead?
options: Analyse how the playwright's language and dramatic methods create effects in the extract
Write about a completely different scene from the play
Summarise the whole play from beginning to end
Focus on the playwright's biography and historical era
questions.explain: Marks come from analysing the writer's methods and their effects, not from copying or narrating the extract.

questions.q: For an essay asking how a character changes over the course of the play, where should evidence come from?
options: References selected from across the whole play showing the character at different stages
A single extract printed on the examination paper
Only the opening scene of the play
A summary of the plot with no textual reference
questions.explain: A whole-text essay on change needs evidence tracing the character through different points in the drama.

questions.q: A character stands alone on stage, voicing their private fears directly to the audience while no one else can hear. Which dramatic technique is this?
options: A soliloquy
A stage direction
Dramatic irony
An act division
questions.explain: Speaking private thoughts aloud while alone on stage is the defining feature of a soliloquy.

questions.q: An extract ends with the stage direction 'She slams the door and storms out.' How might a candidate best use this in analysis?
options: Comment on how the action conveys the character's anger and heightens the moment's tension
Ignore it because only spoken lines can be analysed
Rewrite the stage direction in their own words
Count how many stage directions appear in the extract
questions.explain: Stage directions are part of the playwright's craft and can be analysed for the emotions and effects they create.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Literature in English (0475) syllabus; Paper 3: Drama (Open Text)
